cards.title: Marshall Islands stick charts: three kinds
cards.text: Marshallese navigators made charts from the ribs of palm fronds tied with coconut fibre, with shells for islands. Museums describe three kinds. The mattang is a teaching chart of how swells bend and bounce around an island. The rebbelib shows a whole chain of atolls. The meddo shows one part of a chain. The charts were studied and memorised ashore. They did not go to sea.
cards.limits: The museum and library accounts do not agree on the meddo's exact use, or on whether a mattang's shells stand for real islands. Each chart could be read fully only by the person who made it.

cards.title: Korent Joel and the voyages to Aur
cards.text: Korent Joel (died 2017) was a cargo-ship captain and one of the last traditional Marshallese navigators. He learned from his grandfather on Rongelap. He described a dilep: a line of heaped swells between two atolls that a navigator feels through the canoe. On canoe voyages from Majuro to Aur, scientists' buoys did not pick up what he described, and a physicist suggested the feeling may come from how the boat moves.
cards.limits: The scientists say their instruments may not have been sensitive enough. The navigators and the scientists describe the sea in different terms, and neither account has been fully put into the other's terms.

cards.title: Knowledge held with permission
cards.text: Joseph Genz, an anthropologist who worked with Korent Joel from 2005, reports that navigation knowledge is still under traditional chiefly control, with rules on how it is passed on. Korent took Alson Kelen as a student because they are family. Korent also said it mattered to him that a scientist should check what he knew. Waan Aelõñ in Majel, led by Alson Kelen, has taught young Marshallese to build and sail canoes since 1989.
cards.limits: The rule about chiefly control is reported by an outside researcher who worked with the navigators. This game does not teach how to read the swells. That knowledge belongs to Marshallese navigators to share.

missions.title: The Chart That Stays Ashore
missions.knowledgeQuestion: When an instrument does not detect what a skilled knower feels, what does that show?
missions.stake: The Lantern House is making a new display. If the card says the sticks are the map, visitors will think the knowledge is in the sticks.

journal.title: The Chart That Stays Ashore
journal.text: I read about Marshall Islands stick charts, which were learned ashore and left ashore. A navigator felt a line of swells that the buoys did not show. Some of this knowledge passes only by family and permission. I wrote a display card that says what the chart can and cannot tell a visitor.
